newsitem.title: UK: Tax rises in UK budget will cut PSBR, not demand.
newsitem.headline: Tax rises in UK budget will cut PSBR, not demand.

text.p: Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown's first budget went some way to tackle Britain's fiscal deficit, but with tax rises aimed primarily at corporates, not households, it will not ease the imbalance in the economy.
"Brown has raised a lot of revenue in his budget to assist the public finances, but he has not done a lot to dampen demand," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan.
Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets agreed.
"There were good reasons to raise taxes in the budget but helping the public finances was only a secondary reason. These tax rises completely miss the primary reason, which is to slow demand."

Brown announced tax rises of around six billion pounds in his budget but corporates will pick up around 90 percent of the bill since only around 750 million pounds is directed at the household sector.
Next year the balance is even worse, with 95 percent targeted at corporates and only five percent at households.

"The Chancellor said in his speech he had two aims -- to meet the 'golden rule' and to reduce inflationary pressures without damaging industry and exports. He has delivered on the first, but in terms of rebalancing the economy this budget is a turkey," said Andrew Snowball, UK economist at the Co-operative Bank.
Mackie agreed. "The increase in personal taxation is trivial. Brown has chosen to work on the structural deficit with this budget and done no demand management."
However, the tax rises mean that the public finances are in a very healthy state and the government will probably not have to raise taxes before the next election.

"The tightening was much greater than expected and the PSBR forecasts have come in much lower than expected -- a result of the budget package and probably an upward revision to tax receipts forecasts. It means little need for tax rises looking ahead," said Loynes.
The Treasury forecast the public finances will be back in the black by fiscal year 2000/01, with the surplus rising to 1.4 percent of GDP the next year, equivalent to roughly 13.5 billion stg.
Mackie said this could put the government under intense pressure to increase spending in the years ahead.
"If the public finances are in the black to the tune of 10 billion pounds or more, it will be very hard to justify tough spending targets."

But while the finances benefit near term from favourable timing effects from the windfall tax -- the government will collect around 2.6 billion pounds this year and spend only 200 million pounds -- some commentators said the government was cutting it fine on reserves for extraordinary events.

"We have a very small reserve for panics this year. Brown is raiding the piggy bank very early and this could be dangerous," said Ruth Lea, head of policy unit at the Institute of Directors. "We have a slight concern that he is leaving himself a bit short."
The five billion pound contingency reserve for 1998/99 has been raided to help fund the health service and education, leaving only 2.8 billion pounds for emergencies.
